blocks.text: But although the name צפור tsippor is common to all birds, the Hebrews nevertheless assert that this same name sometimes signifies the sparrow specifically. Kimchi on Psal. LXXXIV, 4: וצפור הוא עוף קטן וקורין לו בלעז פשרא And tsippor (in that place) is a small bird, which in the vernacular (that is, Spanish) they call paxaro (that is, sparrow). Hence Pomarius: קמחי אומר שלפעמים יוקח בעד עוף קטן שקורין לו בלעז פאסרו, Kimchi said that it is sometimes taken for a little bird, which in the vernacular (or Italian) tongue they call passaro. Aquinas: הוא שם מין עוף מה, It is the name of a certain species of bird. And a little later: והוא עוף קטן וידוע, It is a well-known little bird, namely the sparrow. Accordingly, just as Jerome renders it sparrow in Lev. XIV, 4, so too does the old translator in Psal. X, 1, and LXXXIII, 4, and CI, 8, and CIII, 16, and CXXIII, 7, following the Greeks, who render it στρουθίον [strouthion] in those same passages of the Psalms, and in Eccles. XII, 6, and Thren. III, 52. And conversely, the Greek στρουθία [strouthia], that is, sparrows, in Matth. X, 29, and Luc. XII, 6, the Syriac translator renders ܨܦܪܝܢ tsipparin, for which the Arabic has عصافير [ʿaṣāfīr] atsaphiro. For to them عصفور [ʿuṣfūr] otsphur is the sparrow, a word formed from צפור tsippor with a guttural prefixed. Not knowing this, Chamza, a not undistinguished Arab grammarian, thought that the sparrow is called عصفور by a compound word, because عصي وفر [ʿaṣá wa-farra] it strikes and flees. Nor is it peculiar to the Hebrews that they call the sparrow by the same word as they also call larger birds. For the Greek name of the sparrow, στρουθὸς [strouthos], is also used of the hen. Nicander in the Alexipharmaca, line 60:
Ἠέ τι μηελόεντα χαλικρότερον ποτὸν ἴσχοις Ὄρνιθος στρουθοῖο κατοικάδος, — — — [Ēe ti mēeloenta chalikroteron poton ischois / Ornithos strouthoio katoikados]
Or may you have some marrowy, undiluted drinkable remedy from the domestic sparrow-bird, that is, from the hen. And again, line 535:
Ἠὲ πάτον στρουθοῖο κατοικάδος, — — [Ēe paton strouthoio katoikados]

Or the dung of the domestic sparrow, that is, of the hen. Hence it came about that the great Libyan hen, by far the largest of birds, was called στρουθὸς [strouthos], in a word the ostrich. Imitating this, the [II, 723] Roman writers call the ostrich the sea sparrow. Plautus in the Persa, Act 2:
Fly at a run. P. That is what the sea sparrow usually does around the circus.
Cook you the egg of the sea sparrow. [col. 147]

Festus: The sea sparrow, which the common people call the struthiocamelus. The Roman word passer is thought to allude to the Hebrew צפור tsippor and to have arisen from it. But a great man, commenting on Solinus, observes that the sparrow was also called passa, as the female sparrow is called paisse in French. Hence the Glosses: Passa, εἶδος ὀρνέου [eidos orneou]. And passa was formed from the Aeolic πίζα [piza], for σπίζα [spiza]. For σπίζα [spiza] is the finch, a bird similar to the sparrow. Hesychius: Σπίζα· ὀρνιθάριον στρουθῷ παρεμφερές [Spiza: ornitharion strouthō paremferes]. And sometimes it is taken more broadly for a little bird in general, as in Timon, quoted by Laertius, on Arcesilaus:
Οἱ δέ μιν ἠΰ τε γλαῦκα περὶ σπίζαι τερατοῦντο, [Hoi de min ēy te glauka peri spizai teratounto]
